newsitem.title: FRANCE: France on track to submit C. Lyonnais plan to EU.
newsitem.headline: France on track to submit C. Lyonnais plan to EU.

text.p: The French finance ministry said on Friday it was on track to submit a long-delayed privatisation plan for state-owned Credit Lyonnais bank to the European Commission in early April for clearance.
"The plan is in the last stages of finalisation," said a finance ministry spokeswoman, adding that it should be ready for presentation in early April.
The spokeswoman said Finance Minister Jean Arthuis and European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert were in frequent contact by telephone about the proposal.
The government announced in February that it was postponing presentation of the plan, which could cost up to 30 billion francs, after the Commission sought changes to an outline presented by France.
Briefly the world's biggest bank outside Japan, Credit Lyonnais nearly collapsed in the early 1990s after a lending binge led to massive losses.
Just two years ago, the Commission approved a rescue plan of 45 billion francs in state aid for the bank.

While the Commission is expected to press for more disposals in exchange for approving further state aid, Credit Lyonnais chairman Jean Peyrelevade has warned that the bank cannot imperil its future by selling off strategic operations.

The bank, which lost 21 billion francs between 1992 and 1994, recently surprised financial markets by reporting a modest 1996 net profit of 202 million francs but a vastly improved underlying performance, fuelling hopes that its recovery would be quicker than had been anticipated.
Peyrelevade has said he is already meeting the terms of a 1995 state-brokered restructuring plan which obliged the bank to cut its commercial presence outside France by 35 percent.
He said that the bank would return to the size it was in 1998 "before the crazy period started."
The bank has said its recovery plan involved a "strategic recentring" around domestic retail banking and an international banking business geared to large firms and financial markets.
But he hinted in a a recent newspaper report that he could resign if his aim of making the bank viable were jeopardised.

A source close to the discussions said the bank wanted to keep its current presence in Asia, Eastern Europe and North America and would strongly resist any move to sell assets that would trigger big capital losses.
Peyrelevade has explicity ruled for out for the moment selling German bank BfG, which bank sources have said could result in a five billion franc capital loss.
The European Commission is expected to take three to four months to study the plan before giving its verdict.

Published reports suggest the Commission has already accepted the bank's view it cannot spell out publicly what assets will be put up for sale in order to maintain commercial confidentiality. "There will be no urgency," a source close to the talks said.
The bank is expected to have until the end of 1998 to put the new plan into operation. The centre-right government has said it wants to privatise the bank in early 1999.
